- To see the sparse/empty case you can narrow the window constants in `app/flights/page.tsx` temporarily — please restore them.
- Capture screenshots at each viewport.

Report every actionable finding. Do not fix anything.

content.text:
I read the diff, exercised `/flights` in a real browser at three viewports, and measured the things you asked me to measure. Findings below, most severe first.

## What I verified working

- **Page never scrolls sideways.** `document.scrollWidth === clientWidth` at 390, 768 and 1440. The table scroller is the only thing that overflows (phone: 682px content in a 356px container, `overflow-x: auto`). The new coverage line wraps to two lines at 390px and does not break the centred header.
- **No console errors or React warnings** during load, search, filter and clear at any viewport — only HMR/devtools noise.
- **Focus is visible and tab order is logical** (nav → search input → status select), and focus stays on the search input when the table swaps to the empty state.
- **Sparse render is fine** — a 3-row board (search "Rio") just shrinks; no collapsed layout.
- **"search from the home page" points at the right place.** `/book` 307s to sign-in; the home page has the unauthenticated "Find your trip" form. Correct destination.

## Blocking

**1. The empty-state copy tells the user to fix a search they never made — and with the seeded data this is what the status filter *always* does.**
`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:204-213`. Seen at all three viewports; screenshot `shots/desktop-empty-filter.png`, `shots/phone-empty-search.png`.

Select "Delayed" with an empty search box and you get, verbatim:

> 🔍 No flights found
> Try searching for a different destination, origin, airline, or adjust the status filter.
> Showing departures from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days. To book a flight further ahead, search from the home page.

Nothing there is true or useful for what the user did. They filtered by status; they are told to change a search term and to go book a flight.

This is not a corner case after your change. The whole table has exactly one DELAYED (MA202, 2026-06-10) and one CANCELLED (MA303, 2026-07-05) row, and **both now fall outside the window**. So on today's seed, "Delayed" and "Cancelled" are guaranteed dead options — two of the four choices in the status dropdown lead straight to this wrong copy. Before the change they returned a row.

The empty state needs to branch on cause, not render one string for three different situations:
- `flights.length === 0` (window genuinely empty, no user input) — must not say "try searching".
- query set, no match — name the query, and explain the window as the *reason*.
- status filter only — say no flights in this window have that status.

**2. `take: 200` can make the coverage line say something false.**
`app/flights/page.tsx:31-45` feeds `HORIZON_DAYS` to the board unconditionally, so the board asserts "the next 7 days" even on a request where the cap truncated the far end. The comment at line 27-32 acknowledges the cap drops the furthest-away rows; the copy does not. A user searching for a day-6 flight would then get "No flights found" alongside a sentence promising day 7 is covered — the exact failure mode you set out to prevent, just moved. The page knows: `flights.length === MAX_ROWS` means the window was truncated, and either the copy or the last row's date should reflect that.
I could not exercise this — the seed puts 31 rows in the window, nowhere near 200. It is reasoning from the code path, not an observation.

**3. The coverage line fails WCAG AA contrast. Measured, as requested.**
`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:88` — `rgba(255,255,255,0.45)` at `0.9rem` (14.4px computed), normal weight.

- Composited over the actual rendered background at that spot (`rgb(18,14,26)` — body `#0d0c14` plus the `page-container` radial gradient, which *brightens* the background exactly under the header where this line sits): text resolves to ≈`rgb(125,122,129)`, **4.52:1 nominal**.
- Sampled from a 3x device-scale screenshot of the element itself, the brightest glyph pixel is `rgb(121,119,126)` → **4.31:1 actual**, because antialiased glyph edges never reach full alpha.

14.4px normal is not "large text" (needs 18.66px bold / 24px normal), so the threshold is 4.5:1. It sits on the line nominally and under it as rendered. For comparison I measured the subtitle above it at 7.19:1 and the empty-state text (which inherits `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`) at 5.43:1.

The design problem is worse than the number: this is the single sentence that has to be read to avoid "my flight is cancelled", and it is styled as the least important text on the page — smaller and dimmer than the subtitle it is correcting. `rgba(255,255,255,0.6)` measures 6.25:1 and would still read as secondary.

**4. The empty state is not announced.** There is no live region anywhere on the page (`[aria-live], [role=status], [role=alert]` → 0 matches; the `alert` in the aria snapshot is the Next dev overlay). A screen reader user types into the search box, the table is removed from the DOM, and nothing is spoken — focus stays in the input, so they get silence and no way to know the result count changed, let alone that the board only covers a week. `role="status"` on the results container is the minimum here, and it matters more after this change because the range is now the most common reason for zero results.

Related, same block: "🔍 No flights found" is a `<div>` at 1.5rem (`FlightStatusBoard.tsx:206`), not a heading. It looks like one and is not reachable by heading navigation. Page heading order itself is clean — one `h1`, no skipped levels.

## Significant

**5. The top of the board still leads with flights that have already left, all badged "On Time".**
Screenshot `shots/desktop-default.png`, `shots/tablet-default.png`.

Browser clock was 2026-08-05 14:37 America/Los_Angeles. The first four rows are 01:00 AM, 02:30 AM, 10:45 AM, 11:00 AM — departed hours ago. The fifth, 03:00 PM, was 23 minutes away. At 1440x900 the rows occupy y=464 through y=894, so **every row in the first screenful of a board called "Live Flight Status" is a departed or imminent flight**, each carrying a green "On Time" badge, with no "Departed" treatment and no marker of where *now* falls in the list.

You fixed the severe version of this (top row was 2026-05-15). The residual version is the deliberate 24-hour history combined with ascending order, and it still means the answer to "what is leaving next" is not the thing the user sees first. Either mark past departures distinctly, insert a now-divider, or scroll/anchor the board to the next departure. Worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting.

**6. "search from the home page" is plain text, not a link.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:210`. It is the only actionable instruction in the empty state, and it makes the user go find the nav themselves. `next/link` to `/` (correct target, per the redirect check above).

## Copy verdict — your question 2 and 3

**Both placements are right; the verbatim repetition is not.** The header sentence and the empty-state sentence are byte-identical, so the second one reads as boilerplate the eye has already dismissed, and it lands underneath a competing instruction ("try searching for a different destination") that points the user the other way. The two placements have different jobs: the header sets expectation, the empty state diagnoses.

**Does it prevent the "my flight is cancelled" read?** Only partly. "Showing departures from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days." states a fact and leaves the user to derive the consequence. Someone who searched for a flight three weeks out and got nothing has to notice the dimmest line on the page, remember their own departure date, and do the subtraction. Two things would raise the hit rate a lot:

- **Absolute dates, not relative durations.** The user is holding a booking with a date on it. "5–12 Aug 2026" is comparable at a glance; "the next 7 days" is not.
- **State the consequence in the empty state, not the range.** Suggested:
  - Header: `This board covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026.`
  - Empty state (query set): `No flights on this board match "GA999". This board only covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026 — for a flight after that, search from the home page.`
  - Empty state (window empty, no input): `No departures scheduled between 5 Aug and 12 Aug 2026.` — and drop the "try searching" line entirely.
  - Empty state (status filter only): `No flights on this board are marked Delayed.`

**Genuinely-zero-with-no-search is reachable** — I hit the identical render through the Delayed filter (finding 1). I could not narrow the window constants to produce it via an empty query, because I have no editing tools; however `filteredFlights === flights` when the query is empty and the filter is ALL, so an empty `flights` array renders exactly the DOM I screenshotted. Your instinct is right: that wording is wrong for that state.

## Suggestions

**7. `historyHours && horizonDays` is a falsy-zero check.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:31`. Pass `historyHours={0}` for a future-only board and the coverage line silently vanishes from both the header *and* the empty state — the one place it is load-bearing. `!== undefined` is what is meant. Your test "says nothing about a window it was not told about" would pass for the wrong reason in that case.

**8. The `plural` helper only pluralises half the sentence.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:24-25` bakes `the last ` into its return value, so it cannot be used for the days half, which is inlined as a second ternary on line 32. Two different mechanisms for the same job in one string.

**9. The query has no `select`, so 35% of the payload you just measured is fields the board never renders.** Confirmed against the live dev-server query log: `SELECT ... firstClassRows, businessRows, premiumEconomyRows, economyRows, seatPattern`. Measured on today's window: 8779 bytes full vs 5679 bytes with the eight rendered fields selected. Since payload size is the entire point of #153, this is the obvious remaining half of the fix.

## Pre-existing, not introduced here, but in the journey

**10. On a 390px phone the status board does not show status.** Measured column offsets inside the 356px scroller: Flight 0–110, From 110–231, To 231–352 visible; **Departure 352–476, Status 476–582, Price 582–682 entirely off-screen**, with no scroll affordance, shadow or hint. Screenshot `shots/phone-default.png`. Horizontal scroll inside a table is the hardest gesture to discover on touch, and the two columns that answer the page's question are the ones behind it. Not your change, but this change makes the board the authoritative live view, so it is worth a card.

**11. Table has no accessible name and no `scope` on any `th`** (`caption: false, ariaLabel: null, scopeAttrs: [null × 6]`). The search input and status select have no `<label>` — the input's name comes from its placeholder, and the `<select>` has **no accessible name at all** (aria snapshot: bare `combobox`).

## On issue #84

You asked whether the new line makes the contradiction worse. **Yes, measurably.** The three header lines now read in sequence:

> Live Flight Status
> Real-time departures, **arrivals**, and schedule status updates.
> Showing **departures** from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days.

The new line contradicts the word "arrivals" directly above it, and "the last 24 hours" undercuts "Real-time" — previously the false claim was merely unsupported, now it is refuted one line later by the page's own copy. Not a new issue; it does raise the priority of #84, and it argues for fixing the subtitle in the same pass rather than after.

## What I could not exercise

- **The `take: 200` truncation path** — seed puts 31 rows in the window. Finding 2 is code-path reasoning, not an observation.
- **An empty window via an empty query** — no editing tools to narrow the constants. Reproduced the identical DOM through the status filter instead; see finding 1.
- **Loading and error states** — the page is `force-dynamic` with a single server-side `findMany` and no Suspense boundary, `loading.tsx` or `error.tsx` under `app/flights/`, so there is no loading or error UI to review. A Prisma failure renders the global error boundary, which this change does not touch.
- **Real assistive-tech output** — I inspected the accessibility tree and live regions programmatically, not with a screen reader.

Screenshots: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-travel-app/94121201-47c3-4281-aeff-7838379a510d/scratchpad/shots/` — `{phone,tablet,desktop}-{default,full,empty-search,empty-filter,sparse}.png`, `focus-input.png`, `focus-select.png`, and the contrast probes `probe-coverage.png`, `probe-subtitle.png`, `probe-empty-*.png`.

The page knows: `flights.length === MAX_ROWS` means the window was truncated, and either the copy or the last row's date should reflect that.
I could not exercise this — the seed puts 31 rows in the window, nowhere near 200. It is reasoning from the code path, not an observation.

**3. The coverage line fails WCAG AA contrast. Measured, as requested.**
`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:88` — `rgba(255,255,255,0.45)` at `0.9rem` (14.4px computed), normal weight.

- Composited over the actual rendered background at that spot (`rgb(18,14,26)` — body `#0d0c14` plus the `page-container` radial gradient, which *brightens* the background exactly under the header where this line sits): text resolves to ≈`rgb(125,122,129)`, **4.52:1 nominal**.
- Sampled from a 3x device-scale screenshot of the element itself, the brightest glyph pixel is `rgb(121,119,126)` → **4.31:1 actual**, because antialiased glyph edges never reach full alpha.

14.4px normal is not "large text" (needs 18.66px bold / 24px normal), so the threshold is 4.5:1. It sits on the line nominally and under it as rendered. For comparison I measured the subtitle above it at 7.19:1 and the empty-state text (which inherits `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`) at 5.43:1.

The design problem is worse than the number: this is the single sentence that has to be read to avoid "my flight is cancelled", and it is styled as the least important text on the page — smaller and dimmer than the subtitle it is correcting. `rgba(255,255,255,0.6)` measures 6.25:1 and would still read as secondary.

**4. The empty state is not announced.** There is no live region anywhere on the page (`[aria-live], [role=status], [role=alert]` → 0 matches; the `alert` in the aria snapshot is the Next dev overlay). A screen reader user types into the search box, the table is removed from the DOM, and nothing is spoken — focus stays in the input, so they get silence and no way to know the result count changed, let alone that the board only covers a week. `role="status"` on the results container is the minimum here, and it matters more after this change because the range is now the most common reason for zero results.

Related, same block: "🔍 No flights found" is a `<div>` at 1.5rem (`FlightStatusBoard.tsx:206`), not a heading. It looks like one and is not reachable by heading navigation. Page heading order itself is clean — one `h1`, no skipped levels.

## Significant

**5. The top of the board still leads with flights that have already left, all badged "On Time".**
Screenshot `shots/desktop-default.png`, `shots/tablet-default.png`.

Browser clock was 2026-08-05 14:37 America/Los_Angeles. The first four rows are 01:00 AM, 02:30 AM, 10:45 AM, 11:00 AM — departed hours ago. The fifth, 03:00 PM, was 23 minutes away. At 1440x900 the rows occupy y=464 through y=894, so **every row in the first screenful of a board called "Live Flight Status" is a departed or imminent flight**, each carrying a green "On Time" badge, with no "Departed" treatment and no marker of where *now* falls in the list.

You fixed the severe version of this (top row was 2026-05-15). The residual version is the deliberate 24-hour history combined with ascending order, and it still means the answer to "what is leaving next" is not the thing the user sees first. Either mark past departures distinctly, insert a now-divider, or scroll/anchor the board to the next departure. Worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting.

**6. "search from the home page" is plain text, not a link.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:210`. It is the only actionable instruction in the empty state, and it makes the user go find the nav themselves. `next/link` to `/` (correct target, per the redirect check above).

## Copy verdict — your question 2 and 3

**Both placements are right; the verbatim repetition is not.** The header sentence and the empty-state sentence are byte-identical, so the second one reads as boilerplate the eye has already dismissed, and it lands underneath a competing instruction ("try searching for a different destination") that points the user the other way. The two placements have different jobs: the header sets expectation, the empty state diagnoses.

**Does it prevent the "my flight is cancelled" read?** Only partly. "Showing departures from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days." states a fact and leaves the user to derive the consequence. Someone who searched for a flight three weeks out and got nothing has to notice the dimmest line on the page, remember their own departure date, and do the subtraction. Two things would raise the hit rate a lot:

- **Absolute dates, not relative durations.** The user is holding a booking with a date on it. "5–12 Aug 2026" is comparable at a glance; "the next 7 days" is not.
- **State the consequence in the empty state, not the range.** Suggested:
  - Header: `This board covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026.`
  - Empty state (query set): `No flights on this board match "GA999". This board only covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026 — for a flight after that, search from the home page.`
  - Empty state (window empty, no input): `No departures scheduled between 5 Aug and 12 Aug 2026.` — and drop the "try searching" line entirely.
  - Empty state (status filter only): `No flights on this board are marked Delayed.`

**Genuinely-zero-with-no-search is reachable** — I hit the identical render through the Delayed filter (finding 1). I could not narrow the window constants to produce it via an empty query, because I have no editing tools; however `filteredFlights === flights` when the query is empty and the filter is ALL, so an empty `flights` array renders exactly the DOM I screenshotted. Your instinct is right: that wording is wrong for that state.

## Suggestions

**7. `historyHours && horizonDays` is a falsy-zero check.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:31`. Pass `historyHours={0}` for a future-only board and the coverage line silently vanishes from both the header *and* the empty state — the one place it is load-bearing. `!== undefined` is what is meant. Your test "says nothing about a window it was not told about" would pass for the wrong reason in that case.

**8. The `plural` helper only pluralises half the sentence.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:24-25` bakes `the last ` into its return value, so it cannot be used for the days half, which is inlined as a second ternary on line 32. Two different mechanisms for the same job in one string.

**9. The query has no `select`, so 35% of the payload you just measured is fields the board never renders.** Confirmed against the live dev-server query log: `SELECT ... firstClassRows, businessRows, premiumEconomyRows, economyRows, seatPattern`. Measured on today's window: 8779 bytes full vs 5679 bytes with the eight rendered fields selected. Since payload size is the entire point of #153, this is the obvious remaining half of the fix.

## Pre-existing, not introduced here, but in the journey

**10. On a 390px phone the status board does not show status.** Measured column offsets inside the 356px scroller: Flight 0–110, From 110–231, To 231–352 visible; **Departure 352–476, Status 476–582, Price 582–682 entirely off-screen**, with no scroll affordance, shadow or hint. Screenshot `shots/phone-default.png`. Horizontal scroll inside a table is the hardest gesture to discover on touch, and the two columns that answer the page's question are the ones behind it. Not your change, but this change makes the board the authoritative live view, so it is worth a card.

**11. Table has no accessible name and no `scope` on any `th`** (`caption: false, ariaLabel: null, scopeAttrs: [null × 6]`). The search input and status select have no `<label>` — the input's name comes from its placeholder, and the `<select>` has **no accessible name at all** (aria snapshot: bare `combobox`).

## On issue #84

You asked whether the new line makes the contradiction worse. **Yes, measurably.** The three header lines now read in sequence:

> Live Flight Status
> Real-time departures, **arrivals**, and schedule status updates.
> Showing **departures** from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days.

The new line contradicts the word "arrivals" directly above it, and "the last 24 hours" undercuts "Real-time" — previously the false claim was merely unsupported, now it is refuted one line later by the page's own copy. Not a new issue; it does raise the priority of #84, and it argues for fixing the subtitle in the same pass rather than after.

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app
gh issue comment 79 --body "Concrete instance for \"status tables\" and \"no required information is clipped\", measured on \`/flights\` at 390px while working on #153:

Inside the 356px table scroller the columns sit at Flight 0–110, From 110–231, To 231–352 — so **Departure (352–476), Status (476–582) and Price (582–682) are entirely off-screen**, with no scroll affordance, shadow or hint. Horizontal scroll inside a table is among the hardest gestures to discover on touch, and the two columns that answer the page's question are the ones behind it.

Worth prioritising now that #153 makes this board the bounded, authoritative live view rather than a dump of the whole timetable."

gh issue comment 80 --body "Concrete findings on \`/flights\`, measured while working on #153:

- The results \`<table>\` has no accessible name and no \`scope\` on any of its six \`<th>\` elements.
- The search input has no \`<label>\` — its accessible name comes from the placeholder — and the status \`<select>\` has **no accessible name at all** (it surfaces as a bare \`combobox\`).
- The board had no live region, so filtering swapped the table out silently. #153 adds a \`role=\"status\"\` announcing the result count, since being outside the board's window is now the commonest reason for zero rows; the labelling gaps above are untouched and belong here.

Also relevant to \"verify color contrast\": the coverage line #153 adds was 4.31:1 as first written and is now 0.6 alpha (6.25:1). The board's remaining dim text is worth a sweep — the empty-state copy inherits \`rgba(255,255,255,0.5)\` at 5.43:1, which passes but is close."

Second pass on `fix/bound-flight-status-board` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (still uncommitted). You reviewed this page an hour ago and raised findings 1–11. This pass is about whether the fixes hold. Do not re-derive the whole review — focus on the changes, and on anything they might have broken. ## What I changed in response **Your 1 (empty state said the wrong thing, and Delayed/Cancelled were guaranteed dead ends).** The empty state now branches on cause, in `emptyStateMessage()`: - query set → `No flights on this board match “X”. It only covers departures from A to B.` plus a `next/link` to `/` labelled "Search all flights" - status filter only → `No flights on this board are marked Delayed.` - neither → `No departures are scheduled between A and B.` The "Try searching for a different destination…" string is gone entirely. **Your 2 (`take: 200` could make the coverage line false).** The page now derives the end of the stated range from the last row actually returned when `flights.length === MAX_ROWS`, so the copy can never promise more than the board holds. **Your 3 (contrast 4.31:1).** Coverage line is now `rgba(255,255,255,0.6)` at `0.95rem`. ` reporting "N flights shown", and the empty-state "No flights found" is now an `

` rather than a styled `
`. **Your 5 (first screenful was departed flights badged On Time).** `HISTORY_HOURS` dropped from 24 to 6. Marking a departed flight as departed belongs to #84; this only stops the default view being dominated by them. Tell me whether 6 hours is actually enough of an improvement or whether it still leads with departed rows. **Your 6.** "Search all flights" is now a `next/link` to `/`. **Your 9 (35% of payload unrendered).** The query now has a `select` of exactly the eight fields the board renders. **Your 7 and 8** are moot — the `historyHours && horizonDays` falsy check and the half-baked `plural` helper are both gone; the board now takes a single pre-formatted `coverage: { from, to }` prop, formatted server-side with an explicit `en-US` locale so the two renders cannot disagree. **Your #84 point** — the subtitle no longer claims "Real-time" or "arrivals". `, the new link's focus treatment, responsive behaviour of the reworked header and empty state at 390/768/1440. 6. The `select` change means the board receives fewer fields. Confirm nothing renders `undefined` anywhere. Findings 10 and 11 (phone column overflow, table/control labelling) are pre-existing and now tracked on #79 and #80 — don't re-report unless my change made them worse. Screenshots as before. Report anything still wrong.

All green: `tsc --noEmit` clean, 16 tests pass. Worktree restored to its original state (my scratch test file removed). --- # UI review, pass 2 — `fix/bound-flight-status-board` Nine of your eleven fixes hold. Two new defects came in with the rework, both of the same class as the one finding 1 was about — copy that states something the board cannot back up. ## Your six questions, answered first **1. Coverage line contrast: 7.20:1 (worst case). Passes AA and AAA.** Measured by hiding the `

` with `visibility: hidden`, screenshotting its exact bounding box, and compositing `rgba(255,255,255,0.6)` onto the sampled pixels — the `.page-container` radial gradient means there is no single background value. Backgrounds behind the line range `rgb(15,13,23)` to `rgb(19,15,27)`: | bg pixel | composited text | ratio | |---|---|---| | rgb(15,13,23) | rgb(159,158,162) | 7.25:1 | | rgb(18,14,26) (most common) | rgb(160,159,163) | 7.22:1 | | rgb(19,15,27) (brightest) | rgb(161,159,164) | **7.20:1** | 15.2px / weight 400, so normal text: AA needs 4.5, AAA needs 7. Clears both. (My first automated pass reported 7.27:1 by walking computed styles; that ignores the gradient. The pixel figure is the real one.) Evidence: `shots/probe-no-text.png`, `shots/probe-with-text.png`. **2. All three empty states exercised.** B and C are right. A has a grammar defect and D is a new falsehood — see findings below. No stale instruction survives anywhere: `Try searching for a different destination` returns zero matches in the rendered DOM in every state. **3. The live region behaves.** `role="status"` on a `

` that is a *sibling* of the table wrapper, not an ancestor (`inTableContainer: false`, parent has exactly 2 children). Only its own 16 characters are in the announcement; the table is never re-announced. It is present in both states, so the region exists before it updates. Text tracked correctly: `29 flights shown` → `0 flights shown` (Delayed) → `6 flights shown` (search `MA2`) → `1 flight shown` singular. **4. Six hours is the right call, but it does not finish the job on phone.** Measured across 168 hourly samples of the seed: | | mean past rows at top | worst case | |---|---|---| | `HISTORY_HOURS = 24` | 3.9 | 6 | | `HISTORY_HOURS = 6` | **1.0** | **3** | Rows above the fold: desktop 6, tablet 5, **phone 3**. So on desktop the worst case went from "the entire first screen is departed flights" to "one of six" — a real fix. On phone, worst case 3 past rows still fills the whole first screenful, and right now 2 of the 3 phone rows are departed flights badged "On Time" (`shots/phone-default.png`). Keep 6; the residual is the badge lying, which is genuinely #84. **5. Nothing else broken.** Heading order is `H1: Live Flight Status` → `H2: 🔍 No flights found`, no skip. The link takes a visible focus ring (`outline: rgb(167,139,250) auto 3px`) and sits last in DOM/tab order after the input and select, which is the logical position. No horizontal document scroll at 390, 768 or 1440 (`scrollWidth === clientWidth` at all three). Zero console errors or React warnings in the default journey. **6. The `select` is safe.** `flightFareCents` reads only `{ priceCents: number }` (`lib/bookingPricing.ts:31-33`), which the select provides. Across 29 rendered rows: no `undefined`, no `NaN`, no `null`, no `Invalid Date`, zero empty ``s. --- ## Blocking ### 1. A search combined with a status filter blames the search and the date window, when neither is the cause `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:77-83` The `if (query)` branch returns before `statusFilter` is ever consulted. Search `London` (which **is** on the board — MA203 London→New York, 6 Aug) and set the dropdown to Cancelled: > No flights on this board match "London". It only covers departures from Aug 5, 2026 to Aug 12, 2026. Both clauses are false. London matches. The window is not why the row vanished — the status filter is. The user is then offered "Search all flights", which sends them to `/` to re-run a search that was never the problem, while the dropdown they actually need to reset stays where it was. This is the same defect finding 1 was about, moved rather than removed: the message names a cause the user did not create. Seen at all three viewports (`shots/{phone,tablet,desktop}-empty-combined.png`) and reproduced in isolation. The branch needs to consider both inputs — when a filter is active and a query is set, say so. ### 2. The coverage line contradicts the rows it describes, for every user outside the server's timezone `app/flights/page.tsx:43-44` and `:78` versus `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:234-237` Coverage is formatted server-side in the server's timezone with a forced `en-US`. The rows are formatted client-side with the client's timezone and locale. Same page, two clocks: | browser | coverage line says | first row | last row | |---|---|---|---| | America/Los_Angeles (= server) | Aug 5 → Aug 12, 2026 | 8/5/2026 | 8/12/2026 | | Europe/London, en-GB | Aug 5 → **Aug 12**, 2026 | 06/08/2026 | **13/08/2026** | | Pacific/Auckland, en-GB | Aug 5 → **Aug 12**, 2026 | 06/08/2026 | **13/08/2026** | | Asia/Tokyo, ja-JP | Aug 5 → **Aug 12**, 2026 | 2026/8/6 | **2026/8/13** | An Auckland user reads "this board covers departures to Aug 12" while looking at a row dated 13/08/2026, and reads a start of Aug 5 above a first row of 06/08. The formats disagree too — `Aug 5, 2026` against `06/08/2026`. This sentence exists specifically so a user holding a booking can compare its date against the board; in most of the world it cannot be compared. This is new, because the coverage line is new. The underlying bare `toLocaleDateString()` in the table is pre-existing, but it only became a correctness problem once a differently-formatted range was placed above it. Two visible side effects, both confirmed: - `pageerror: Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client.` — an uncaught error on the changed page for any non-server timezone. - Because React only regenerates on re-render, the dates **silently change** on first interaction: MA404 renders as `8/5/2026 10:45 AM`, and after typing a single character into the search box it becomes `06/08/2026 05:45`. Evidence: `shots/desktop-auckland-after-rerender.png`. Fixing the range to match the rows means picking one clock and one formatter for both. ### 3. "between Aug 5, 2026 **to** Aug 12, 2026" is ungrammatical `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:89-91` The no-query/no-filter state renders: > No departures are scheduled between Aug 5, 2026 to Aug 12, 2026. `between … to` should be `between … and`, or reuse the `from … to` phrasing the other two branches already use. The new test at `__tests__/components/FlightStatusBoard.test.tsx` asserts this exact string, so it currently locks the error in — fix both. Not reachable from the seeded window (29 rows always present), so I rendered the component directly with `flights={[]}` to reach it. That is the one state I could not confirm in a browser; the reason is data, not a gap in the journey. --- ## Suggestions, not blocking - **The status-filter empty state offers no context and no exit.** "No flights on this board are marked Delayed." is true and correctly scoped — the blocking half of finding 1 is properly fixed. But it never mentions the window, so a user who filtered Delayed does not learn that a delayed flight next month simply is not here. The coverage line is still on screen above, which is why this is a suggestion rather than a defect. - **Truncation still overclaims the final day.** `app/flights/page.tsx:72-73` takes the last row's date as `coverage.to`. If the cap lands mid-day, the board holds departures up to (say) 15:00 on Aug 8 but claims it covers "to Aug 8, 2026". Much smaller than the original problem, and unreachable on the seed (29 rows against a 200 cap), but the same shape. - **The emoji is now inside a heading's accessible name.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:261` — promoting the div to `

` was right, but screen readers now announce "magnifying glass tilted left, No flights found" when navigating by heading. Move the 🔍 into an `aria-hidden` span. - **The live region fires per keystroke.** Typing "London" produced `16 flights shown` then five consecutive `6 flights shown`. Polite queuing makes this tolerable, and I would not debounce it without evidence, but it is worth knowing. - **The way out disappears with the coverage prop.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:263` gates the "Search all flights" link on `searchQuery.trim() && coverage`. Rendered without `coverage`, a fruitless search shows no link at all — the link's usefulness does not depend on whether a range is known. --- ## Not re-reported Findings 10 and 11 (phone column overflow, table/control labelling) are unchanged by this work and remain on #79/#80. The table still has no accessible name in the populated state — the new `

` exists only in the empty state — but that is #80's scope, not a regression. ## Coverage gaps - The **no-rows-at-all** state (finding 3 above) was verified by direct component render, not in the browser: the seeded window always returns 29 rows and I would not mutate your database to empty it. - The `MAX_ROWS = 200` truncation path was likewise not exercised in the browser for the same reason; the unit test covers it. - MCP Playwright could not launch (it wants a Chrome channel at `/opt/google/chrome/chrome` that is not installed), so all browser work ran through the bundled Chromium via direct Playwright scripts. Same engine, same results. Screenshots are in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-travel-app/94121201-47c3-4281-aeff-7838379a510d/scratchpad/shots/`: `{phone,tablet,desktop}-default.png`, `-empty-statusfilter.png`, `-empty-query.png`, `-empty-combined.png`, plus `desktop-empty-query-linkfocus.png`, `desktop-auckland-after-rerender.png`, `probe-with-text.png`, `probe-no-text.png`.

input.content:
Found while bounding the flight status board (#153). Pre-existing, but that change
is what makes it matter.

**Verification status:** confirmed with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` against the seeded
database.

## The plan

`/flights` now selects a range of `departureDate`. Postgres has no index that can
serve it:

```
Seq Scan on "Flight"  (rows=30 loops=1)
  Filter: (("departureDate" >= $1) AND ("departureDate" <= $2))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 1390
Execution Time: 1.588 ms
```

The only candidate is `@@unique([flightNumber, departureDate])`, which leads with
`flightNumber`, so a range predicate on the second column cannot use it.

## Why it matters now rather than before

1.6ms across 1420 rows is nothing, and before #153 the page had no predicate at all
— it read the whole table by design. The justification for the `take: 200` cap that
#153 adds is explicitly that a real timetable is denser than the seed. At that
density this query is a sequential scan over everything, on a `force-dynamic` page
that runs it per request.

So the cap protects the payload and leaves the scan unbounded. Both halves want the
same index.

## Fix

An index on `Flight.departureDate`. Worth checking which other paths filter or sort
on it before choosing between a plain index and a composite — flight search and the
schedule occurrence generator are the likely other readers, and a composite that
serves all three is better than three indexes.

Migrations here are hand-authored SQL (`prisma/schema.prisma` plus a matching file
under `prisma/migrations/`), so this needs both.

input.content:
`/flights` ran `findMany` with no `where` and no `take`, serialising every row into
the RSC payload on every request — **1420 rows, 404 KB**, spanning May 2026 to
August 2027, on a page that answers "is my flight on time". Ascending order meant
the top of the board was the oldest departure in the database.

Now: a window of the last 2 hours through the next 7 days, `take: 200`, and a
`select` of only the eight columns the board renders. **30 rows, 5.5 KB — 73×
smaller.** Measured before and after, and confirmed independently by the verifier.

## Choosing the history window

Two hours rather than a day, because nothing advances `Flight.status` when a flight
leaves. Every row of history is therefore a row asserting "On Time" about a
departure that has already gone — worse than being absent, since absent reads as
ambiguous and "On Time" reads as answered.

```
history= 2h -> 28 rows,  1 departed and badged On Time
history= 6h -> 30 rows,  3
history=24h -> 32 rows,  5
```

Two keeps the case worth having — "did my flight actually leave?" — at one
misleading row until #84 marks a departed flight as departed. The 7-day horizon
holds: one day is 7 rows, two weeks is 57 and starts reaching back toward the
timetable.

## A board holding a window has to say so

Otherwise a search for a flight next month returns nothing and reads as "your flight
is missing". Two `ui-review` passes found the copy was the hard part:

- **The empty state blamed causes the user hadn't created.** One string told a
  customer who had only touched the status dropdown to "try searching for a
  different destination". This is not a corner case: with the window applied, the
  only DELAYED and CANCELLED rows in the whole table fall outside it, so **two of
  the four dropdown options were guaranteed to hit that copy**. It now answers the
  actual cause — search, status filter, both, or an empty window.
- **The both-inputs case needed to know which input was to blame.** A search for
  "London" with Cancelled set was answered "no flights match London" — while London
  *was* on the board and the filter had removed it. It now checks whether the query
  matches ignoring the filter, and raises the window only when the query is genuinely
  the reason.
- **Dates were the wrong unit.** I stated an absolute range first; the reviewer
  measured that the rows format client-side in the viewer's timezone while a
  server-formatted range does not, so an Auckland reader saw "covers to Aug 12"
  above a row dated 13/08 — plus a hydration error and dates silently changing on
  first keystroke. Correct timezone display needs the airport reference #84
  introduces, so the range is a duration: same sentence in every timezone.
- Contrast on that line measured **4.31:1 → 7.20:1**, a visually-hidden
  `role="status"` announces the result count, "No flights found" is an `<h2>` with
  the emoji in an `aria-hidden` span, and the way out is a real link.
- The subtitle no longer claims "Real-time" or "arrivals" — there is no feed and no
  arrivals column, and the new coverage line refuted both one line later. Now pinned
  by a test, which the verifier noticed it wasn't.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (564 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`, and the full Playwright suite — 28 passed, workers:1, no retries,
so every pass is first-attempt.

The verifier ran the new tests against the previous page and component: **13 of 18
fail**. It also flagged that `reads the soonest departures first` passes against the
old code — the old page already ordered ascending, so that one is a characterization
test, not coverage of this fix. Worth knowing rather than counting.

It caught one thing worth repeating: `e2e/admin.spec.ts:239` asserts a newly-delayed
flight appears on `/flights`, which now depends on `HORIZON_DAYS`. It passes because
that spec ticks all seven weekdays, but shortening the horizon below ~2 days would
break it.

`departureWindow()` exists because `Date.now()` in a component body trips
`react-hooks/purity` — a real lint error I introduced. No disable comment; the
window still moves per request, verified by calling the page twice 1.1s apart.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#167** — `Flight.departureDate` has no index, so this is a seq scan
  (`Rows Removed by Filter: 1390`). Harmless at 1.6ms today, but the whole
  justification for `take: 200` is that a real timetable is denser, and at that
  density the cap protects the payload while the scan stays unbounded.
- Concrete call sites added to **#79** (phone: Departure, Status and Price columns
  are entirely off-screen with no scroll affordance) and **#80** (table has no
  accessible name or `th` scope; the status `<select>` has no accessible name at
  all).

content.text:
#153 is fixed and merged as `cb80e03`.

## The measurement

**1420 rows / 404 KB → 30 rows / 5.5 KB.** A 73× payload reduction, confirmed independently by the verifier. The board now queries the last 2 hours through the next 7 days, caps at 200 rows, and selects only the eight columns it renders.

## Two hours of history, not a day

Nothing advances `Flight.status` when a flight departs, so every hour of history is a row asserting "On Time" about a flight that has already gone:

```
history= 2h -> 28 rows,  1 departed and badged On Time
history= 6h -> 30 rows,  3
history=24h -> 32 rows,  5
```

"Not listed" reads as ambiguous; "On Time" on a departed flight reads as answered and wrong. Two hours keeps the case worth having — *did my flight actually leave?* — at one misleading row until #84 marks departures as departed.

## The copy was harder than the query

Bounding the data was ten lines. Two `ui-review` passes found the consequences:

- **The empty state blamed causes the user hadn't created.** One string told someone who had only touched the status dropdown to "try searching for a different destination." Not a corner case — with the window applied, the only DELAYED and CANCELLED rows in the entire table fall outside it, so **two of four dropdown options led straight to that copy**.
- **The both-inputs case needed to know which input was at fault.** Searching "London" with Cancelled set was answered "no flights match London" — while London *was* on the board and the filter had removed it. It now checks whether the query matches ignoring the filter.
- **I chose the wrong unit for the range.** Absolute dates seemed better — you're holding a booking with a date on it — but the rows format client-side in the viewer's timezone while a server-formatted range doesn't. An Auckland reader saw "covers to Aug 12" above a row dated 13/08, plus a hydration error and dates silently changing on first keystroke. Durations are the same sentence everywhere.

Also: contrast 4.31:1 → 7.20:1 on that line, a live region announcing the result count, and the subtitle no longer claims "Real-time" or "arrivals" — there's no feed and no arrivals column, and the new line refuted both one line later.

## Worth knowing

The verifier ran the new tests against the old code: 13 of 18 fail. It also caught that one of mine — `reads the soonest departures first` — passes against the old page, since it already ordered ascending. That's a characterization test, not coverage of this fix, and I'd rather say so than count it.

Filed **#167**: `Flight.departureDate` has no index, so this is now a seq scan (`Rows Removed by Filter: 1390`). Harmless at 1.6ms, but the justification for `take: 200` is that a real timetable is denser — at that density the cap protects the payload while the scan stays unbounded. Also added concrete call sites to #79 and #80 rather than filing duplicates.

Five merged this session: #157, #161, #164, #166, #168. The cheap bucket is down to **#158** (`GEMINI AIRWAYS` on the boarding pass, with a case-sensitive test that misses it) and **#160** (third copy of the leg label) — both small and adjacent. After that it's the Phase 2 chain starting at #73, which needs your decisions from #143 before any SQL gets written.

Found by the `ui-review` pass on #158, which changed the wordmark beside it. Both
pre-date that change.

**Verification status:** measured in the rendered app at 390x844 with a real
booking.

## 1. The boarding pass prints the raw enum

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1368` renders the cabin badge as
`{p.cabinClass}`, so a customer's e-ticket reads:

```
PREMIUM_ECONOMY
```

Underscore and all. "Premium Economy" is what belongs on a printed pass; the enum
shape is an implementation detail leaking onto the most customer-facing artefact the
app produces.

`CABIN_LABELS` already exists in the same file, but its values carry fare suffixes
("Premium Economy (+50%)") because they are written for the cabin picker, so this
needs a plain display name rather than that map as it stands.

## 2. The banner has no gap, so at 390px the two halves touch

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1358` lays the banner out with
`justifyContent: 'space-between'` and no `gap` and no `flexWrap`. Measured with
`PREMIUM_ECONOMY`, the badge consumes 141px of a 274px banner, the carrier name
wraps to two lines ("MONA" / "AIRWAYS"), and the gap between the name and the badge
is **0px** — they are flush against each other.

The two are related: fixing (1) removes most of (2), since "Premium Economy" is
narrower than `PREMIUM_ECONOMY` and the wrap stops happening. A `gap` on the banner
is still worth adding so the two can never touch regardless of the strings.

Measured for comparison at the same viewport: with `ECONOMY` the name fits on one
line with a 17px gap, so this is specific to the longer cabins.

## Why it is worth doing

This is the artefact a customer screenshots and shows at an airport. It is also the
one part of the app where the wording cannot be corrected after the fact by
re-rendering — people keep the picture.

input.content:
The boarding pass on checkout step 4 — the e-ticket a customer keeps and shows at
an airport — hardcoded `GEMINI AIRWAYS` with an `alt="Gemini"` logo, long after #72
and #138 consolidated the product identity everywhere else.

The guard that existed to prevent exactly this matched `/Gemini Airways/`, so a
shouted spelling and a bare `alt` both walked straight past it. It passed while the
string shipped.

## The fix

The span renders `BRAND.name.toUpperCase()`. The guard now matches `/gemini/i`.

**It also scans `.prisma` now.** `prisma` was already in the directory list, but the
extension list was `.ts`/`.tsx`, so the whole directory contributed exactly one file
— `seed.ts`. `schema.prisma` is shipped source that can carry the name in a
`@default`, where nothing else would ever see it. The verifier found this after I
had convinced myself the scan's scope was fine.

Both halves are directionally tested rather than assumed:

- The pattern, against the pre-change component: fails with exactly one offender,
  the boarding pass. The old pattern passes against the same bug.
- The extension, against a temporarily mutated `schema.prisma`: caught.

## A bare pattern can fire on something innocent

`/gemini/i` is blunt, deliberately — requiring "airways" would reintroduce the
`alt="Gemini"` half of the hole. But the word is a constellation, a NASA programme
an Orlando city guide could plausibly mention, and a model family. Someone enriching
`CityGuideData.ts` would hit a test named *"carries no carrier name other than the
product"* and see a bare filename.

So the failure message now says what to do:

```
Old carrier name found in: <files>. If this is the product identity leaking,
use BRAND from lib/brand.ts. If the match is legitimate, add the file to
ALLOWED at the top of this test.
```

`ALLOWED` is a named list — previously the `lib/brand.ts` exemption was an inline
filter with no obvious home for a second entry.

## alt=""

The carrier is named in full immediately beside the image, so alt text could only
duplicate it — announcing the airline twice per pass, per leg, per passenger.
`ui-review` confirmed against the live accessibility tree that the card still
conveys the carrier.

Worth stating plainly, because this fix makes it *silent* rather than fixed:
`public/img/logo.svg` still draws "Gemini" as vector paths, so a sighted customer
still sees that mark beside the words MONA AIRWAYS. That is #140, blocked on design
work, and out of scope here — but a screen reader now says the right thing while the
picture does not, so no text-based check will ever flag it again.

I looked at the assets while I was there and added two findings to #140: the site
background `public/img/gemini-background.jpg` is a photograph with **"Gemini
Airways" painted along the aircraft fuselage**, so renaming the file would satisfy a
filename check while leaving the wordmark on screen; and the logo is recognisably a
third party's brand mark, which raises that issue above cosmetic.

## Verification

`npm run lint` (0 errors), `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (564 unit + 21 database),
`npm run build`. `ui-review` exercised a complete round-trip booking to the
confirmation step at phone, tablet and desktop in both `ECONOMY` and
`PREMIUM_ECONOMY` (the widest badge) — no defects, and the shorter name actually
improves the phone layout by 9px of clearance.

Playwright was judged unwarranted by both sub-agents and by me: no e2e spec
references the carrier name, and the two specs that reach the boarding passes assert
on flight numbers and seats.

## One fixture changed

`BookingCheckoutWizard.test.tsx` used `airline: 'Gemini Airways'` as flight data.
Harmless today — the pass does not render the operator — but the new negative
assertion would fail on that fixture the moment a boarding pass starts showing the
operating carrier, and it would read as a brand regression rather than test data.
It is `'Test Air'` now.

The remaining `'Gemini Airways'` fixtures across the suite stay: the verifier
checked each assertion site and they exercise the `airline` *column*, not product
identity. One of them is an airline filter checkbox, which needs a carrier that is
not the product for the test to mean anything.

## Filed rather than fixed

- **#169** — the boarding pass prints the raw enum `PREMIUM_ECONOMY`, underscore and
  all, on a customer's e-ticket; at 390px that badge takes 141px of a 274px banner
  and butts against the carrier name with a 0px gap
- Added the `titlebar.tsx` duplicate-announcement case to **#80** — it does the
  opposite of this change, `alt={BRAND.name}` beside a visible name

content.text:
#158 is fixed and merged as `76c2f55`.

## What shipped

The boarding pass names the product via `BRAND`, and the guard now matches `/gemini/i` instead of `/Gemini Airways/` — a shouted spelling and a bare `alt="Gemini"` had both walked past it while the string shipped on every customer's e-ticket.

**The guard also scans `.prisma` now.** The verifier caught something I'd talked myself out of: `prisma` was already in the directory list, but with `.ts`/`.tsx` extensions the whole directory contributed exactly one file — `seed.ts`. `schema.prisma` is shipped source that can carry the name in a `@default` where nothing else would see it. I mutation-tested both halves rather than assuming: the pattern against the pre-change component (one offender, the right file), and the extension against a temporarily mutated schema (caught, then restored).

Since `/gemini/i` is deliberately blunt — requiring "airways" would reintroduce the `alt` half of the hole — the failure message now tells you to exempt the file rather than reword prose. The word is a constellation, a NASA programme an Orlando city guide could mention, and a model family.

## The part worth your attention

**This fix makes the remaining problem silent rather than solved.** `public/img/logo.svg` still draws "Gemini" as vector paths, so a screen reader now says "MONA AIRWAYS" while a sighted customer still sees the old mark beside it. No text-based check will ever flag that again.

While looking at the assets I found two things worse than #140 records, and commented there:

- `public/img/gemini-background.jpg` — the site background — is a photograph with **"Gemini Airways" painted along the aircraft fuselage**. Renaming the file would satisfy any filename check while leaving the wordmark on screen, so I deliberately didn't.
- The logo is recognisably a third party's brand mark, which puts #140 above cosmetic.

#140 is blocked on design work — it needs a replacement mark or none, and inventing one isn't mine to do.

## Also

Filed **#169**: the boarding pass prints the raw enum `PREMIUM_ECONOMY`, underscore and all, and at 390px that badge takes 141px of a 274px banner and butts against the carrier name with zero gap. That's the artefact people screenshot.

One fixture went neutral (`'Test Air'`) because the new negative assertion would have failed on it as a brand regression the moment a pass starts showing the operator. The rest stay — the verifier checked each assertion site and they exercise the `airline` column, not identity; one is a filter checkbox that needs a carrier that *isn't* the product.

Six merged this session. The cheap bucket is down to **#160** (third copy of the leg label — small, and it's prep for #131). After that: #140 needs a design decision from you, and the Phase 2 chain from #73 needs the migration-ownership and policy calls listed in #143.

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

input.prompt:
Review new product identity artwork on branch `design/product-identity-assets` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app (uncommitted — `git status` plus `git diff`). AGENTS.md step 6.

This is a **design** review as much as a UI one. I designed these assets myself and I want an independent eye. Be blunt — if something looks amateurish, cheap, or off-brand, say so plainly. I would rather hear it now.

## The problem being solved

Issue #140. `public/img/logo.svg` was **Google's Gemini brand mark** — a third party's trademark shipping as this product's logo. `public/img/gemini-background.jpg` was a photo with "Gemini Airways" painted along the aircraft fuselage, used as the home hero. `app/favicon.ico` was still the Vercel triangle from `create-next-app`. No OG image existed, so shared links showed nothing.

## What I made

1. **`public/img/logo.svg`** — the new mark. An M drawn as one continuous path split at its valley into two strokes: outbound bright, return dimmer. The monogram and a two-leg itinerary are the same shape, which is the product's own domain object (`ItineraryLeg`). Square viewBox, because the old asset was 344x127 requested at 20x20 and 32x32 and painted as a 7px sliver. No wordmark in the asset — both call sites already name the airline in adjacent text.
2. **`app/icon.svg`** — favicon. Same M knocked out of a gradient badge, because a tab strip can be light or dark and the bare mark would sink into one.
3. **`app/apple-icon.png`** — 180x180, square (iOS applies its own mask).
4. **`public/img/hero-routes.svg`** — replaces the photo. Ambient route arcs with node dots and two radial glows. A photograph cannot be redrawn and a stock substitute would say nothing, so the hero is built from what the product is made of: routes between places.
5. **`public/img/og-image.jpg`** — 1200x630 social card, rendered from the real typeface (Outfit).
6. `app/layout.tsx` gains `openGraph`/`twitter` metadata and `metadataBase`.

`app/favicon.ico` and the old JPG are deleted.

## What I want judged

1. **Is the mark any good?** Look at it at 20px (boarding pass), 32px (site header), and large. Does it read as an M? Does the two-tone split read as intentional or as a rendering bug? Does it look like a real airline mark or like a default? Compare against the wordmark text beside it — does the lockup balance?
2. **The hero.** I tuned it twice: the SVG paints its own dark base, so the CSS overlay had to be lightened, and at ≤900px I dim it further because `cover` scales the arcs up until they cross the form inputs. Check both breakpoints. Is the art too faint to bother with, too busy, or right? Do the arcs ever reduce legibility of the search form or the headline?
3. **The OG card** — `public/img/og-image.jpg`. Open it directly. Composition, typography, whether it would look right in a Slack/iMessage unfurl.
4. **The favicon at real size.** 16px in a tab. Does the M survive, or is it mud?
5. **Coherence.** Do these five assets read as one identity, and do they belong with the existing app (Outfit type, purple/magenta palette, dark UI)?
6. **Anything broken**: the boarding pass banner at step 4 of checkout still uses the mark at 20px; the header uses it on every page. Contrast, responsive behaviour, console errors.

## Practical

- Postgres may need `docker compose up -d db mailpit`. `npm run dev` on :3000 — **port 3000 is currently free and `.next` was just rebuilt**, so start a fresh server.
- `e2e/booking.spec.ts` has a full journey to the boarding pass if you want to see the mark at 20px in situ.
- Screenshots at phone/tablet/desktop.

Do not fix anything — report. If you think a specific shape, colour or size is wrong, say what you would change it to.

content.text: Dev server stopped, worktree restored to exactly the state I found it in (my scratch spec and `test-results/` removed). ## Screenshots All under `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-travel-app/94121201-47c3-4281-aeff-7838379a510d/scratchpad/`: `home-phone.png` `home-tablet.png` `home-desktop.png` `tablet-card.png` `desktop-card.png` `results-desktop.png` `results-phone.png` `journey-after-select.png` `pass-desktop.png` `pass-phone.png` `banner-4x.png` `marks.png` `marks-zoom.png` `mark-big.png` `tab-16.png` `og-sizes.png` `empty-desktop.png` --- # Blocking ## 1. The hero art runs through the search form, and its node dots land *inside* the controls `app/globals.css:198-217`, `public/img/hero-routes.svg:48-52` Seen at **desktop 1440x900** and **tablet 768x1024**, initial hero state. The CSS comment says "On a wide screen the routes run beside the card". They do not. At 1440x900 an arc cuts diagonally through the FROM select and continues through the TO select, and a filled node dot (`circle cx="902" cy="566" r="4.5"`) sits **inside the FROM combobox**, on the value baseline between "Chicago, USA" and the chevron. At 768 the same dot lands on the "Chicago, USA" text baseline. See `desktop-card.png` and `tablet-card.png` (3x crops). I measured it rather than eyeballed it: screenshotting with and without the background and diffing luminance, the brightest artwork pixel inside the card bbox is at **(455,439) at tablet — inside the FROM control's own rect** (202–566 × 430–452), and 0.125 luminance delta at desktop. This is not a contrast failure. White value text over the lit arc is still ~5.4:1. It is a *truth* failure: a filled circle of the same diameter and near the same weight as the ROUND TRIP / ONE WAY radios above it is sitting in a select, and it reads as UI — a bullet, a stray glyph, a disabled radio, dirt on the screen. What I would change: keep the arcs, move the dots. A line crossing a translucent card reads as atmosphere; a dot reads as content. Relocate all five `` elements out of the central 40% horizontal band of the 1600×900 canvas (they are currently at cx 860–1240, i.e. 54–78%, which is exactly where a centred 480px card lands after `cover`). Alternatively give `.search-trip` an opaque backdrop instead of `rgba(255,255,255,0.03)`. ## 2. `.home` is not the hero — it is the entire `/` page container, results included `components/ui/flightBookingForm.tsx:735` (`className="page-container home"`) Both the CSS comment and the `≤900px` rule reason about "the hero". The selector's actual blast radius is the whole search journey. Seen at **desktop**, results state (`results-desktop.png`, `journey-after-select.png`): the art also covers the flight results list, the Modify Search card and the Filters card. A node dot lands on the outbound result card's bottom edge under "Book Now"; arcs cross the TO, DEPART, RETURN and CABIN CLASS controls and the Filters card. `background-size: cover` on an element that grows with content makes this worse, not better: at phone the `.home` box is **1240px tall** for a 16:9 image, so the SVG is scaled to 2204px wide and cropped — which is the exact failure the `≤900px` rule was written to prevent, still happening, just on a taller page. Two honest halves to this: in the wide empty region right of the results list the art is genuinely good and fills what used to be dead space. Behind form controls it is a liability. The rule needs to be about *where on the page*, not *how wide the viewport is*. ## 3. Header logo has a doubled accessible name `components/ui/titlebar.tsx:106` ```tsx {BRAND.name} ``` Both inside one ``. Computed link name: "Mona Airways Mona Airways". This change is what made it wrong — the new mark deliberately carries no wordmark, so the alt is now pure duplication of the adjacent text. The same reasoning already produced `alt=""` on the boarding pass (`BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1344-1348`); it was not carried across. Should be `alt=""`. ## 4. `/favicon.ico` now 404s `app/favicon.ico` deleted; only `app/icon.svg` replaces it. Verified: `curl /favicon.ico → 404`, `/icon.svg → 200`. Browsers follow the emitted ``, but crawlers, feed readers and several chat clients request `/favicon.ico` by path. Add `app/icon.png` (Next emits a second ``) or restore a 32x32 `.ico` rendered from the new badge. --- # Design defects ## 5. The favicon at 16px is mud — and it is the return leg that dies `app/icon.svg:17` — `` `tab-16.png` renders it at true 16px in simulated Chrome light and dark tab strips, with an 8x nearest-neighbour zoom. The badge decision is correct — it holds contrast against both strips. The glyph does not. 62% white over the badge gradient is **2.15–2.58:1 against its own background**; at 16px both counters close to roughly one pixel and the right stroke becomes a pale smear. It reads as "Λ" with a blur, not an M. Two compounding problems: the M is only **17.4/32 = 54% of the badge width**, so it floats with too much padding for a mark this simple. Concretely, what I would change: - Both strokes solid `#fff`. A 16px glyph can carry one idea; the two-leg story belongs to the large mark. - Feet to `x=6.5` and `x=25.5`, apexes to `y=9`, feet to `y=23.5`, `stroke-width="4"`. That gets the M to ~62% of the badge and opens the counters. ## 6. At 20px on the boarding pass the two-tone split reads as a rendering bug `components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:1349`, colours from `public/img/logo.svg:28` `banner-4x.png` is the real banner (same gradient, same 12px/20px padding, same 0.8rem letter-spaced caps) at 4x. The right leg is visibly half-erased and its descending stroke nearly disappears at the foot. The banner ground is `linear-gradient(135deg,#1e1b4b,#311042)` under `rgba(0,0,0,0.2)`, i.e. `#18163c`→`#270d35`; the return gradient's end `#6d4bb8` measures **2.75–2.80:1** against it. You asked directly whether it reads as intentional or as a bug. At 20px on that ground: bug. At 32px in the header and at 64px+ it reads as intent. I would lift the return gradient to roughly `#9b6fe0` → `#7c5ad0` — about 3.3–4.4:1 on the banner, still unmistakably the quieter leg beside `#a78bfa`→`#d946ef`. ## 7. The mark's hierarchy inverts on white, contrary to the comment in the file `public/img/logo.svg:19-23` The comment claims: *"this mark sits on near-black, on the boarding pass indigo, and on white. Fixed values look the same on all three."* Measured: | | on `#0d0c14` | on white | on `#312e81` | |---|---|---|---| | outbound `#a78bfa` | 7.15 | **2.72** | 4.20 | | outbound `#d946ef` | 5.62 | 3.46 | 3.30 | | return `#8f5ad8` | 4.28 | 4.54 | 2.51 | | return `#6d4bb8` | 3.10 | **6.27** | **1.82** | On white the *dimmer return* becomes the dominant stroke and the *bright outbound* fades below the 3:1 non-text floor. See the "on white" panel of `mark-big.png` — it's obvious. On the indigo the return leg is 1.82:1, effectively gone. This matters practically: there is no `@media print` block anywhere in `app/globals.css`, and browsers drop background gradients when printing by default, so a printed e-ticket *is* the white case. Either restrict the claim in the comment to dark grounds, or anchor the outbound darker (`#7c3aed` → `#c026d3` works on both). --- # Design opinion, since you asked for blunt **Is the mark any good?** Yes, at 32px and above. It reads as a wide-set geometric M. The strokes are consistent, the inner strokes are correctly steeper than the outer (21° vs 18.4°) which is what makes it read as an M rather than a mountain range, and the valley resolves cleanly because the bright stroke is painted over the dim one — the overlap looks like layering, not like a seam. It does not look like a default and it is not amateurish. It *is* generic in the way most modern travel marks are generic — a gradient monogram — but it is competently drawn. **Where it's weak geometrically.** It uses only **22.4 of 32 vertical units** (5.3 top, 4.3 bottom) while filling **26.4 of 32 horizontally**. It's a squat, wide M floating in a square box, and at 20px the effective cap height is 14px. I would rebalance to roughly `x 4→28`, `y 5→27`, `stroke-width 4.6` — about 20% more apparent size exactly where it is struggling. Also, ink centre is at y=16.5 against a box centre of 16, so it sits half a unit low. **Lockup.** At 32px against 1.2rem bold Outfit, it balances well — the mark's optical weight is right, neither shouty nor apologetic. But the *wordmark* is set three different ways across the identity: title-case bold in the header, ALL CAPS bold letter-spaced on the boarding pass, ALL CAPS light widely letter-spaced on the OG card. **That is the biggest coherence gap in the set — the mark is consistent and the wordmark isn't.** The OG treatment is the best-looking of the three; the header needs small-and-bold. Pick two and retire the third (the boarding pass's). **The hero.** Right idea, right restraint, wrong placement. It is not too faint to bother with on desktop. On phone it is effectively invisible — a flat purple wash above the fold and one faint arc below (`home-phone.png`, `results-phone.png`). The ≤900px rule dimmed it past the point of contributing anything, so on phone you are paying for an HTTP request and getting a gradient. I would rather the phone rule kept the two radial glows and dropped the arcs entirely than keep arcs at ~14% visibility. **The OG card.** The best of the five. Composition, hierarchy and type are right; it survives to 220px and the headline still reads at 120px (`og-sizes.png`). JPEG quality is fine — clean at 2x zoom, no ringing on the white headline at 52KB. Two notes: the right 55% is empty, defensible as negative space but reads as unfinished at large unfurl width. And the card's headline repeats `og:title` verbatim, so a Slack unfurl will stack "Mona Airways — Where Your Journey Takes Flight" as text directly above an image saying "Where your journey takes flight" in *different casing*. Drop the tagline from the image (mark + subtitle is enough) or reword the title. **The favicon badge decision is right.** The gradient badge survives both a light and a dark tab strip, which the bare mark would not have. Only the glyph inside it is wrong. --- # Checked, nothing to report - **Horizontal scroll**: none. `scrollWidth === clientWidth` at 390, 768 and 1440 on home, results, checkout and the boarding pass. - **Console**: clean on home at all three viewports and through the full booking journey. One `Failed to load notifications: TypeError: network error` fired during context teardown after viewport resizes — unrelated to this diff. - **Focus**: the logo link is the first tab stop and shows a visible `rgb(243,243,243) auto 2px` outline at 1px offset on the dark header at both phone and desktop. - **Headline contrast over the new glow**: worst case is the `#c084fc` gradient end over the dawn glow peak (`#46307a`) = **4.05:1**. At 3.2rem/800 that is large text needing 3:1 — passes. Worth knowing it halved from 7.36:1 on the old flat ground. - **Social metadata**: complete set emitted, including `og:image:alt`, width/height, `twitter:card=summary_large_image`. `metadataBase` resolves absolute URLs correctly. - **apple-icon.png**: 180x180, 8-bit RGB with **no alpha channel** (correct for iOS), square with no baked corner radius (correct — iOS masks). Gradient matches `icon.svg` within 1–2/255 at sampled points. The blur I first thought I saw was a 2x-screenshot artefact; edge-transition counts across a horizontal slice are identical to the SVG rasterised at the same size. - **Hero node dots sit on their paths**: each `` centre is an actual on-path endpoint of its `Q…T` arc. That detail is right, and it's the kind of thing that would have been easy to fudge. - **Reduced motion**: genuinely N/A — none of the five assets animate. --- # What I could not exercise - **A two-leg round-trip boarding pass.** The seeded return (MA102) departs the same day as MA101 and my scripted return-selection didn't land within the time I gave it; I fell back to a one-way booking (MA101 Seattle→Detroit, seat 11B, `pass-desktop.png`). The mark renders identically per leg so the mark review is unaffected, but "does the two-leg pass say the true thing" is a gap. - **A genuine "no flights found" empty state.** My no-result query params were reset by the form to the default route, so I got the initial hero back (`empty-desktop.png`). The `.home` background is identical in that state so finding #1 carries, but I did not see the empty-results panel itself. - **Real Safari/iOS rendering** of `apple-icon.png` and the SVG favicon — assessed by rasterisation in Chromium only. - **Print preview.** I established there is no `@media print` rule, which is what makes the white-ground case in finding #7 real, but I did not render a print preview of the boarding pass. - **`app/apple-icon.png` has no test.** The new `identity assets` block in `__tests__/docs/productIdentity.test.ts:97-104` asserts `logo.svg`, `og-image.jpg`, `hero-routes.svg` and `app/icon.svg` exist — apple-icon.png is the one asset referenced purely by filesystem convention, with no import to break, so it is the one most likely to vanish silently.
